summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring OSI network layer protocols over PPP.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers connect over a PPP line, this step lets them agree to carry a different family of network messages, called OSI.

questions: ppp osi network layer control protocol
how does ppp carry osi packets
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree to carry OSI network layer packets, plus one option for memory alignment.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry many network-layer protocols, but each needs a way to be switched on and configured on a link. OSI protocols also have an awkward habit of landing on odd memory boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: OSINLCP reuses the LCP packet exchange to open and configure OSI on a PPP link, uses PPP protocol field values 0x8023 for control and 0x0023 for data, and offers one option, Align-NPDU, to negotiate how the packet is aligned.
tldr.outcome: It is the Network Control Protocol that lets OSI protocols such as CLNP, ES-IS and IS-IS run over PPP. The memo says nothing about security.

today: RFC 1377 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1992, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: PPP and Its Network Control Protocols
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) has three parts: a way to encapsulate datagrams over serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the data link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring each network-layer protocol.

Both ends first exchange LCP packets to set up the link. Then PPP must send NCP packets to choose and configure one or more network-layer protocols. Once each chosen protocol is configured, its datagrams can flow. This RFC defines the NCP for OSI network layer protocols, called OSINLCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Two phones first agree to talk, then agree on which language to use. This document is the part where they agree on the OSI language.

sections.title: OSI Network Layer Protocols over PPP
sections.content:
The RFC reviews which OSI network layer protocols suit PPP. They are told apart by the first octet of each packet, the Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID) from ISO/TR 9577, so no extra discriminator is needed below the network layer. The value zero, the "Inactive Network Layer Protocol", MUST NOT be used over PPP.

The Connection-Oriented Network Protocol (ISO 8208) needs a reliable data link, so PPP's unreliable service is not appropriate for it. The ConnectionLess Network Protocol (CLNP) is a simple unreliable datagram service much like IP and fits PPP well.

For routing, the RFC walks through ES-IS, IS-IS and IDRP. Their periodic hellos and holding timers cope with loss. For very unreliable links the ES-IS Holding Timer may need to be slightly more than three times the Configuration Timer. IS-IS needs a Holding Time greater than k times the ISISHello timer, with k chosen so that losing k consecutive hellos is rare. IDRP has its own built-in reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Some kinds of messages are fine if a few get lost because they get repeated anyway. Those work well on PPP. Others need every message to arrive, so PPP is not a good fit for them.

sections.title: How OSINLCP Works
sections.content:
OSINLCP is responsible for configuring, enabling and disabling the OSI protocol modules on both ends of the link. It is exactly the same as LCP with a few exceptions. Packets may not be exchanged until PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and any received earlier should be silently discarded.

  • One OSINLCP packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 8023.
  • Only Codes 1 through 7 are used (Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject). Other Codes should get a Code-Reject.
  • Implementations should be ready to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination before timing out, and should give up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.

OSI has no option for exchanging network addresses. Instead the ES-IS protocol, ISO 9542, should be used to learn the neighbor's addresses and whether it is an End System or an Intermediate System.
sections.plainLanguage: It uses the same handshake as the first step of PPP, just with its own label on the envelope. Addresses are not swapped here; the computers learn them in another way.

sections.title: Sending and Aligning OSI Packets
sections.content:
Before any OSI packets (NPDUs) are sent, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and OSINLCP must reach the Opened state. Each frame carries exactly one NPDU, with the Protocol field set to hex 0023. The maximum NPDU length equals the maximum Information field length; larger NPDUs must be segmented.

OSI is often carried over data links with odd-length headers, while PPP defaults to even-length headers, so a packet may start on an inconvenient memory boundary. The fix is leading zero padding. A sender MAY insert one to three zero octets between the PPP header and the NPDU, which reduces the maximum NPDU length accordingly. A receiver MUST remove them, and MUST be able to accept any alignment.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine shelves where boxes must start at certain marks. If a box would start in the wrong spot, you slip a little spacer in front so it lines up. The receiver just takes the spacer out.

sections.title: The Align-NPDU Option
sections.content:
OSINLCP has one configuration option, type 1, Align-NPDU, with length 3 and a one-octet Alignment field. It lets a receiver ask for a particular alignment, since the biggest time cost of re-aligning is at the receiver. It is negotiated separately in each direction. A receiver that does not need alignment MUST NOT request it, and a sender that wants alignment SHOULD Configure-Nak with an appropriate value.

The Alignment value is the offset of the NPDU from the start of the PPP header. Values 1 through 4 ask for that offset modulo 4. The value 255 asks for an odd offset (1 or 3), and 254 for an even offset (2 or 4). A sender that cannot vary its padding dynamically MUST NAK with one of the two specific values.

The request is advisory: failing to agree MUST NOT stop OSINLCP reaching Opened. If you accept the peer's alignment option, you MUST send with the agreed alignment. The RFC recommends achieving alignment through header compression where possible; for example an alignment of 3 can come from uncompressed Address and Control fields (2 octets) plus a compressed Protocol field (1 octet).
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can say "please start your box this far from the edge." It is only a polite request, so the two sides can still work together if they disagree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Any protection would have to come from elsewhere in PPP, such as the Authentication phase that precedes the Network-Layer Protocol phase.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not talk about locks or safety, so any of that is handled somewhere else.
